sweep_summary: Tirma-Chai (suri1267, Surmic) is not in the catalog. All four works with stress in the title are false matches: they are attached to suri1267 in Glottolog only because their titles share the word 'Disentangling' with Unseth 1997 'Disentangling the two languages called Suri' (SIL archive 36342); Ogden & Local 1994 is a Firthian-prosodies theory note (no Surmic language), Trofimovich & Isaacs 2012 is L2 foreign-accent research, and Glottolog 618365/618339 are one CUP typology chapter by Gordon (2014) recorded twice. No item bears on Suri word stress; all priority none. Beyond the list, the only open first-hand source reachable today was Bender 1977 (SAL Supp. 7, downloaded and read): group-level, no Suri data, tone said to be grammatical and 'correlated with stress and/or length' in other Surmic languages. Snippet evidence already held by the project from the access pass shows the two real descriptions, Last & Lucassen 1998 (p. 381: 'Chai has distinctive tone.. two tonal levels, with downstep and downdrift') and Bryant 2023 (p. 834: 'a two-tone system that most likely involves a downstep'), describe a tone language and contain no word-stress placement statement (in-volume searches for stress/accent/penultimate return 0 hits). No first-hand statement of stress placement for Tirma-Chai was read, so the best new statement is not found. Acquisition priorities: Bryant 1999 MA thesis (UTA/UMI, print/ILL), Moges Yigezu's ULB dissertation on Surmic phonetics/phonology (no record found online), and the full text of Last & Lucassen 1998. ULB DI-fusion, MavMatrix, HathiTrust and web.archive.org unreachable.

new_statements.rule_in_words: The primary describers analyse Tirmaga-Chai as a two-level (register) tone language with downstep/downdrift, tone carrying mostly grammatical load (verb person/mood, post-verbal subject case); none of the accessible descriptions (Bryant 2023 chapter, Last & Lucassen 1998 as far as indexed, Last & Lucassen 2003 EAE, Smith 2018) makes any statement about word stress or accent placement, and in-volume searches show the word 'stress' is absent from Bryant 2023's chapter.
new_statements.exceptions: None; Last & Lucassen 1998:414 note only a sentence-level extra-high tone on the final syllable(s) of questions (intonation, not word stress).
new_statements.domain_note: Tone statements concern the word/lexeme and verbal inflection; no word-level stress domain is described. Quotes are Google Books snippets of the primary sources (snippet JSON saved), not full-page reads; silence on stress is verified for Bryant 2023 by whole-volume search and for Smith 2018 by full text, but only partially for Last & Lucassen 1998 (snippet view, 3-result cap) and not at all for Bryant 1999/2013.
new_statements.identity_note: Sources describe the two named varieties separately: Bryant (1999, 2013, 2023) describes Tirmaga (Tirma), Last & Lucassen (1998, 2003) describe Chai (Cai); both are suri1267 'Tirma-Chai' (ISO suq), which Bryant 2023 treats as one language 'Suri (Tirmaga-Chai)' whose main phonological difference is the /tʃ/–/ʃ/ contrast in Chai. EAE1 (Last & Lucassen 2003) and Girard 2002 treat Chai, Tirma and Mursi as mutually intelligible dialects of one language; Mursi is a separate Glottolog language (murs1242) already handled elsewhere and its descriptions (Turton & Bender 1976, Worku 2020/2021) were not used as evidence here. Not to be confused with Kacipo-Balesi/Baale 'Suri' (kaci1244) or with suri1273 Surigaonon (Austronesian).

sources.note: Ch. 2 (pp.18-24) summarises Suri phonology after Bryant 1999/2013 and Last & Lucassen 1998 (consonants, seven vowels, lengthened vowels non-phonemic, orthography, segmental processes). Tone appears only as grammatical marking ('post-verbal subjects are often marked with tone as well as with a suffix. Since tone is not usually marked in the orthography..', fn.24 p.31; ex. (62) p.48 'whose only case marking is tonal'). The word 'stress' does not occur anywhere in the thesis.

sources.citation: Gordon, Matthew (2014). Disentangling stress and pitch accent: A typology of prominence at different prosodic levels. In van der Hulst, Harry (eds.), Word Stress. Theoretical and Typological Issues., 8–118. Cambridge, Cambridge University Press.
sources.access_detail: open copy posted by the author (located 2026-09-25); a digital copy (available on request)
sources.note: Suri, Tirma(ga), Chai, Mursi, Surmic, Ethiopia and Nilo-Saharan do not occur anywhere in the chapter (whole text searched; the only string hits for 'chai' are in 'trochaic'). The chapter is a cross-linguistic typology of word stress vs phrasal pitch accent built on Chickasaw, English, Onondaga, Indonesian, French, Chuvash, Cayuga, Nubi, Korean, Wolof and other named cases, plus counts from Hyman (1977), Gordon (2002) and StressTyp (Table 3.1, printed p. 106). Nothing bears on the catalog's lexical-tone entry for Suri.
